paras: The attempted lynching of Paul Doe took place at Brackettville, Texas, in March 1903, when about 150 soldiers gathered at the town jail with picks and crowbars to take out and lynch Doe, a Black youth accused of stabbing a cavalry private. Major Kendall of Fort Clark dispersed the soldiers with a strong guard, and military guards were then posted at the jail. Headlines in papers from Texas to Rhode Island stressed that the would-be lynchers were soldiers, and the Richmond Planet, a Black weekly, reprinted the story.

According to a dispatch dated at Brackettville, Private William Bayne of Troop H, Twelfth Cavalry, was "dangerously stabbed by a negro boy" on a Saturday night, March 14. The dispatch did not describe the circumstances of the stabbing or give the boy's age. Paul Doe was arrested and jailed for it; most headlines treated him as the assailant, while the Providence News called him "Accused of Wounding Private Payne."

After the arrest, about 150 soldiers gathered around the jail with picks and crowbars "to take him out and lynch him." Learning of the trouble, Major Kendall of Fort Clark went down with a strong guard and dispersed them. Military guards were afterward kept about the jail and patrolled the town's streets "to prevent trouble." A "Texas Items" column in the Brownsville Daily Herald summed up the night as an attempt by "a mob of soldiers" that was prevented by "a detachment from Fort Clarke."

The reports called the private's wound dangerous but gave no later word on his condition. No report of a hearing, indictment or trial of Doe appears in the coverage, nor any account of discipline for the soldiers who gathered at the jail.

Nearly all coverage reproduced a single wire dispatch, which circulated in slightly different versions dated March 15, 16 and 17. Texas papers such as the Waxahachie Daily Light and the Bryan Morning Eagle ran it under "Irate Soldiers," with the subhead "They Attempt to Lynch a Negro Who Stabbed One of Them," which stated the charge as fact. Elsewhere the headlines read "Soldiers Try to Lynch Negro" in the Beatrice Daily Express, "Soldiers Menace Negro" in the Omaha Daily Bee and "Stabbed by Negro Boy" in the Waterbury Evening Democrat. Other papers named the crowd outright, as in the Butler Weekly Times' "Soldiers in a Lynchers' Mob," and a German translation in the La Crosse Nord Stern was headed "Lynchmord verhindert" (lynching prevented). None of these papers added comment on the soldiers' conduct or named any of the men at the jail.

The only Black-press item found is in the Richmond Planet of March 21, 1903, headed "Soldiers Tried to Lynch Boy." Its text matched word for word the version that white weeklies such as the Fredericksburg Free Lance, the Milford Chronicle and the Middleburgh Post printed under the same headline, down to the name "Major Rondall." The Planet printed the item without comment, among other brief news.

Copies of the dispatch disagree on several details. The wounded soldier is William Bayne in the Beatrice, Omaha and Nord Stern versions but William or W. M. Payne in the Waxahachie, Providence and Richmond Planet versions. The Omaha Daily Bee dated its dispatch March 15 and placed the stabbing the night before, consistent with the Texas version's Saturday night, while the Nord Stern, dated March 17, said it happened "gestern Abend" (last night). The Nord Stern also gave the crowd as about 160 soldiers rather than 150, and the officer appears as Major Kendall in most copies but as "Major Rondall" in the version the Richmond Planet carried.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of Paul Doe
bases: About 150 soldiers gathered at the Brackettville jail with picks and crowbars to take out and lynch Paul Doe, held for a stabbing, and were dispersed before reaching him (A1, A3, A14).

The mob of about 150 soldiers acted without authority on an accusation of stabbing a comrade, but it was dispersed and no report says Doe was killed or hurt (A1, A4, A14); it was an attempted lynching.

Every report, including the Black-press copy and the Brownsville digest, derives from one Brackettville wire dispatch in slightly varying versions (A1, A3, A13, A14); no independent local or follow-up account was found.
